articles.title: Por que Europa pediu a seus cidadãos para fazerem kits de emergência? | G1
articles.standfirst: No Reino Unido, a recomendação é que cada família tenha condições de sobreviver por pelo menos três dias sem depender de ajuda externa.
articles.summary: No Reino Unido, a recomendação é que cada família tenha condições de sobreviver por pelo menos três dias sem depender de ajuda externa.
articles.body:
O objetivo é garantir que a população consiga se sustentar sozinha por um determinado período caso ocorram interrupções graves nos serviços essenciais.

A medida - que não é exatamente nova ( leia mais abaixo ) - faz parte de uma estratégia de preparação para crises, elaborada em resposta a um cenário cada vez mais marcado ataques cibernéticos , eventos climáticos extremos, guerras e outras situações que podem interromper temporariamente serviços essenciais.

O cenário fez com que a própria Comissão Europeia recomendasse que os Estados-membros sensibilizem suas populações sobre a importância de se preparar para uma catástrofe natural ou outras situações de emergência.

"Todos os cidadãos europeus devem saber como agir, como proteger as suas famílias e como ajudar os outros. A preparação começa nas nossas casas, nas nossas escolas e nas nossas comunidades", disse em comunicado a comissária europeia para a Gestão das Crises, Hadja Lahbib, na semana passada.

As novas diretrizes europeias também preveem a introdução da preparação para emergências nas escolas, por meio de capacitação específica para os professores e atividades que ensinem as crianças e os adolescentes a agir diante de situações de perigo.

Mas antes mesmo do alerta público da Comissão, muitos países já tinham seus próprios planos esquematizados e divulgados.

No Brasil, a Defesa Civil também emitiu avisos sobre preparação para emergências , mas logo esclareceu que a recomendação é preventiva e não há qualquer desastre específico em vista.

No Reino Unido , o governo lançou no final de outubro a campanha "Be Ready" (Esteja Preparado, em tradução livre), no que especialistas classificaram como uma tentativa de "correr atrás" do tempo perdido. Segundo analistas, o país está anos atrás de outras nações europeias em termos de preparação.

A recomendação aos britânicos é que cada família tenha condições de sobreviver por pelo menos três dias sem depender de ajuda externa.

O kit sugerido inclui água potável, alimentos não perecíveis, lanternas, pilhas, carregadores portáteis para celular, rádio, medicamentos essenciais e cópias de documentos importantes.

A campanha também incentiva que cada residência tenha um plano para situações de emergência, incluindo formas de contato entre familiares caso as redes de comunicação sejam afetadas.

Mas o período para qual os cidadãos devem se preparar varia de acordo com o país.

Na Suécia , por exemplo, as autoridades recomendam que os moradores estejam preparados para viver por pelo menos uma semana sem ajuda externa.

O governo distribuiu milhões de exemplares de uma cartilha explicando como agir em cenários de guerra, crises graves ou interrupções prolongadas de serviços essenciais.

A Alemanha adota uma postura ainda mais cautelosa, com orientações da agência federal de proteção civil sugerindo que as famílias mantenham reservas suficientes para 10 dias, incluindo água, alimentos, medicamentos e outros itens de primeira necessidade.

França e Holanda também orientam os moradores a manter reservas básicas para aproximadamente 72 horas.

O plano europeu ganhou força após a invasão da Ucrânia pela Rússia e diante das crescentes preocupações com a segurança do continente.

Também pesaram episódios recentes de enchentes, incêndios florestais, tempestades e interrupções em sistemas digitais que afetaram diferentes países.

Durante o Fórum da Proteção Civil Europeia no início de novembro, a Comissão Europeia destacou que a preparação não deve ser vista como sinal de alarmismo, mas como uma medida preventiva semelhante à contratação de um seguro . As recomendações tampouco são obrigatórias para os membros.

"Não estamos em guerra, mas também não estamos em paz. Vivemos em uma perigosa zona cinzenta, e essa zona cinzenta pode se tornar vermelha num piscar de olhos", alertou a comissária europeia Hadja Lahbib, ressaltando que a União Europeia deve estar preparada para "o pior, inclusive um conflito armado na Europa ".

Vendas de enlatados e conservas subiram 37% no Reino Unido após lançamento da campanha 'Be Ready' — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

No Reino Unido , o secretário de Defesa, Wes Streeting, afirmou que a recomendação não foi motivada por nenhuma "informação de inteligência específica", mas sim pelo objetivo de aprimorar a "resiliência nacional" de modo geral.

O anúncio do governo britânico foca em eventos climáticos extremos, que estão se tornando mais frequentes devido às mudanças climáticas. Mas Streeting também mencionou a ameaça de "ataques cibernéticos cada vez mais sofisticados" contra empresas, bem como a interrupção de cadeias de suprimentos provocada por "atores estatais hostis ou terroristas".

Em entrevista ao jornal The Telegraph , o secretário de Defesa afirmou ainda que o Reino Unido tem pouco mais de 1.000 dias para se preparar, já que Rússia pode reunir, até 2030, capacidade militar e econômica suficiente para um ataque.

Lucy Easthope, especialista em planejamento para desastres e professora na Universidade de Durham, disse à BBC que vem pressionando o governo do Reino Unido a lançar esse tipo de campanha há "cerca de 16 anos".

Segundo ela, sucessivas administrações têm demonstrado receio em "divulgar informações que possam gerar tensão", mas é importante garantir que os próprios cidadãos estejam preparados para facilitar a atuação dos serviços de emergência caso seja necessário.

"Se as pessoas tiverem seus medicamentos para o coração para um período adicional de 48 horas, isso evita que [as equipes de emergência] precisem encontrar, de imediato, um farmacêutico de plantão", disse.

Já na Suécia e na Finlândia , a preparação da população está diretamente ligada à segurança nacional e à deterioração das relações entre a Europa e a Rússia após a invasão da Ucrânia em 2022.

No caso finlandês, o tema ganha ainda mais relevância por causa da extensa fronteira compartilhada com o território russo.

O país, aliás, é frequentemente apontado como um dos mais preparados do continente e mantém há décadas uma cultura de preparação para emergências que envolve cidadãos, empresas e órgãos públicos.

Embora cada país possa adaptar as orientações à sua realidade, as sugestões para os kits de emergência europeus geralmente incluem água potável, alimentos não perecíveis, medicamentos de uso regular, lanternas, baterias, carregadores, rádio portátil, dinheiro em espécie e cópias de documentos importantes.

E embora a recomendação da Comissão Europeia fale em estocar alimentos e outros suprimentos para sobreviver por três dias, não significa que uma crise duraria apenas esse período.

Segundo a estratégia europeia, as 72 horas representam um limite mínimo considerado crucial para a resposta inicial a emergências.

É o intervalo durante o qual sistemas de transporte, energia, telecomunicações ou abastecimento podem sofrer interrupções antes que medidas de contingência sejam totalmente implementadas.

Governo britânico lançou a campanha 'Be Ready' em outubro — Foto: Governo do Reino Unido

No Reino Unido , os alertas já começaram a mudar o comportamento dos consumidores. Dados da empresa de pesquisa de mercado Worldpanel by Numerator mostraram que, nos dez dias seguintes ao lançamento da campanha "Be Ready", as vendas de água engarrafada aumentaram 67%, enquanto as de alimentos enlatados e conservas cresceram 37%.

As compras de álcool em gel registraram alta de 83%, e o número de pessoas adquirindo carnes enlatadas aumentou 43%.

Segundo analistas da empresa de pesquisa de mercado, os números indicam que a população tem seguido as recomendações do governo, embora não haja sinais de corrida aos supermercados ou compras por pânico.

Necessidade de se preparar 'não é de agora'

Alertas como esses não são exatamente uma novidade na Europa , que tem um longo histórico de convivência com conflitos e mantém estruturas de defesa civil mais desenvolvidas do que muitas outras regiões do mundo.

Mas mesmo em períodos recentes, recomendações para uma preparação básica não são incomuns.

A Alemanha , por exemplo, apresentou sua primeira estratégia abrangente de defesa civil desde o fim da Guerra Fria em agosto de 2016.

O plano orientava os cidadãos a manter estoques de água e alimentos suficientes para vários dias em caso de ataques, desastres naturais ou falhas graves de infraestrutura.

Em 2018, a Suécia redistribuiu para cerca de 4,8 milhões de residências uma versão atualizada da cartilha"Om krisen eller kriget kommer" ("Se a crise ou a guerra chegar"), com orientações sobre como os cidadãos deveriam se preparar para interrupções prolongadas no abastecimento, apagões, ataques cibernéticos e até conflitos armados.

Os governos francês e dinamarquês também já orientavam seus cidadãos sobre a importância de um kit básico de sobrevivência antes de 2026.

A própria Comissão Europeia já havia publicado, em março de 2025, uma estratégia conjunta para todos os tipos de ameaças cujo objetivo era aproximar e harmonizar práticas que já existiam em vários países do bloco.

articles.title: Marinha dos Estados Unidos pune marinheiro que pulou de porta-aviões em meio à guerra contra o Irã | G1
articles.standfirst: Jovem de 19 anos estava a bordo do USS Abraham Lincoln, que ficou quase um ano em missão. Quando o incidente aconteceu, ele já estava há 255 dias em alto-mar, e o navio enfrentava falta de alimentos.
articles.summary: Jovem de 19 anos estava a bordo do USS Abraham Lincoln, que ficou quase um ano em missão. Quando o incidente aconteceu, ele já estava há 255 dias em alto-mar, e o navio enfrentava falta de alimentos.
articles.body:
Foto de arquivo: o porta-aviões USS Abraham Lincoln durante a operação Fúria Épica, de EUA e Israel contra o Irã. — Foto: Marinha dos EUA/Divulgação via Reuters

A Marinha dos Estados Unidos puniu e dispensou um marinheiro de 19 anos que pulou de um porta-aviões no Mar Arábico durante a guerra contra o Irã. Nicholas McKelvey passou 255 dias a bordo do USS Abraham Lincoln, em uma missão marcada por jornadas exaustivas , escassez de alimentos e dificuldades para receber atendimento de saúde mental .

A instituição o acusou de simular uma crise psicológica para deixar o serviço militar , segundo reportagem publicada pelo jornal "The New York Times".

McKelvey foi considerado culpado e recebeu uma dispensa geral sob condições honrosas. Com a decisão, ele perdeu o direito ao auxílio educacional do programa GI Bill, benefício que poderia financiar seus estudos universitários.

O caso levantou questionamentos sobre a maneira como as Forças Armadas americanas lidam com problemas de saúde mental entre seus integrantes, especialmente em períodos de missões prolongadas e sob condições extremas.

Especialistas ouvidos pelo "New York Times" questionaram se a Marinha priorizou a punição do militar em vez de investigar e tratar o sofrimento psicológico que pode ter provocado o episódio.

"Eu não queria mais estar lá. Se eu fosse morrer por causa disso, que assim fosse", disse McKelvey ao jornal, em sua primeira entrevista pública sobre o caso.

O marinheiro pulou do porta-aviões em 3 de agosto, de uma altura de aproximadamente 20 metros. Ele foi resgatado por uma equipe de helicóptero e retornou ao navio cerca de 50 minutos depois.

Na época, McKelvey trabalhava como mecânico de aviação em um esquadrão de helicópteros. Cumpria turnos de 12 horas no convés de voo, sob calor intenso e exposto à fumaça das aeronaves.

Ele também enfrentava problemas pessoais. Sua esposa havia dado à luz a segunda filha do casal quatro dias antes do início das operações de combate contra o Irã. Além disso, ele estava preocupado com a saúde dos sogros, que enfrentavam câncer, e não conseguia manter contato regular com a família.

Porta-aviões USS Abraham Lincoln, dos Estados Unidos, ao chegar à Tailândia em setembro de 2026 após passar quase 300 dias em alto-mar. — Foto: REUTERS/Chalinee Thirasupa

Segundo McKelvey, no fim de junho, ele procurou atendimento na unidade médica do porta-aviões para tratar de sua saúde mental, mas foi orientado a conversar com um capelão. Ele recusou a orientação porque considerava que o religioso não era um profissional especializado em saúde mental.

O marinheiro também afirmou que um comandante havia prometido tentar retirá-lo do navio por via aérea, o que não aconteceu. Enquanto isso, o período de serviço do Lincoln foi prorrogado várias vezes.

O episódio ocorreu em meio a um período particularmente difícil para a tripulação do USS Abraham Lincoln. O porta-aviões, que transportava mais de 5 mil militares, permaneceu em missão por quase 322 dias, um recorde para a embarcação.

Uma carta enviada pela Marinha a parlamentares no mês anterior à reportagem informou que houve oito tentativas de suicídio durante o período de serviço do navio . Um dos episódios descritos no documento envolvia um marinheiro que caiu ao mar, descrição compatível com o caso de McKelvey, mas não deixava claro se era ele.

Após o resgate, o militar ficou sob vigilância para prevenção de suicídio e passou por uma avaliação psiquiátrica. Segundo sua esposa, Samantha Larry, ele foi questionado sobre o motivo do salto e respondeu que queria voltar para casa.

McKelvey deixou o porta-aviões em 10 de agosto e passou por diferentes países antes de retornar aos Estados Unidos. Depois de uma internação hospitalar de quatro dias, voltou a trabalhar em uma base naval, onde recebeu tarefas de limpeza, pintura e manutenção.

Em 25 de agosto, foi informado de que a Marinha o acusava de simular uma doença e de abandonar seu posto. Posteriormente, a acusação de ausência sem autorização foi substituída pela de ter saltado da embarcação.

Durante uma audiência, o comandante responsável pelo caso considerou o marinheiro culpado. A Marinha não respondeu diretamente às perguntas específicas do "New York Times" sobre a situação de McKelvey . Em declaração ao jornal, um porta-voz afirmou que os porta-aviões contam com equipes multidisciplinares de saúde mental, responsáveis por oferecer atendimento a diferentes condições.

Ex-advogados militares e especialistas ouvidos pelo jornal divergiram sobre a decisão. Alguns consideraram que a resposta disciplinar tinha justificativa legal, já que a simulação de doença pode ser tratada como infração militar. Outros questionaram se a instituição deveria ter priorizado o tratamento psicológico ou uma dispensa médica que preservasse os benefícios do marinheiro.

A esposa de McKelvey criticou a postura da instituição. Para ela, a Marinha preferiu responsabilizar o militar pelo episódio sem considerar as condições que o levaram a pular do navio.

"Eles não querem assumir a responsabilidade pelo que aconteceu com ele, nem com os outros marinheiros no barco", disse Samantha Larry ao "New York Times".

Ela afirmou ainda que a punição terá consequências para toda a família. O casal, que tem dois filhos pequenos, planeja voltar para Jacksonville, na Flórida, e terá de reorganizar a vida sem o benefício educacional que esperava usar para pagar a faculdade dele.

"Vamos ter que recorrer aos empréstimos estudantis. Isso basicamente nos colocará em uma situação de endividamento", afirmou. "O que eles fizeram foi errado", disse Larry. "Eles preferem culpar a vítima."

articles.title: Lobo-guará é flagrado 'passeando' em parque do Paraná | G1
articles.standfirst: Espécie está em perigo de extinção. Animal foi visto por visitante em trilha que leva à 'floresta de pedras' do Parque Vila Velha.
articles.summary: Espécie está em perigo de extinção. Animal foi visto por visitante em trilha que leva à 'floresta de pedras' do Parque Vila Velha.
articles.body:
Lobo-guará foi visto no Parque Vila Velha (PR) em 14/11/2026 — Foto: Glacy Macedo/imagem cedida pelo parque

Um lobo-guará foi flagrado "passeando" pelo Parque Vila Velha em Ponta Grossa , nos Campos Gerais do Paraná, na manhã deste sábado (14).

O animal estava caminhando livremente no ponto 1 da trilha dos arenitos, cujas rochas formam uma "floresta de pedras" esculpidas por 180 milhões de anos .

Quem o viu foi uma visitante do parque, que estava fazendo birdwatching, como é chamada a prática de observação de aves.

"O maior canídeo da América do Sul é um dos animais mais emblemáticos do Cerrado brasileiro e sua presença também reforça a importância da conservação de ambientes naturais. Além de sua aparência característica, com suas longas pernas e pelagem alaranjada, o lobo-guará desempenha um papel importante no equilíbrio dos ecossistemas. A espécie contribui para a dispersão de sementes, especialmente por meio da alimentação de frutos, e ajuda a manter a dinâmica da vegetação nativa", destacam os responsáveis pelo parque.

O Parque Vila Velha fica na margem da BR-376, a cerca de 17 km da entrada de Ponta Grossa e a aproximadamente 90 km da capital Curitiba.

O espaço é uma unidade de conservação ambiental e possui, ao todo, mais de 3,8 mil hectares, ou seja, 38 milhões de m², área equivalente a mais de 5,3 mil campos de futebol.

O parque abriga uma grande diversidade de fauna e flora, incluindo espécies ameaçadas de extinção, como o puma ou onça-parda (Puma concolor), o lobo-guará (Chrysocyon brachyurus) e a águia-cinzenta (Urubitinga coronata), por exemplo.

articles.title: FBI warns companies in the US and across the world; names AI hacking tool criminals are using to attack financial services; suggests dos and don'ts
articles.summary: Hackers are increasingly deploying autonomous artificial intelligence tools to execute high-speed cyberattacks across the United States and around the
articles.body: Hackers are increasingly deploying autonomous artificial intelligence tools to execute high-speed cyberattacks across the United States and around the globe, according to a flash cybersecurity advisory issued by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The warning highlights a wave of recent intrusions targeting major sectors—including government, defense, telecommunications, law, technology, and finance—with major fallout already documented across South Korea’s financial industry and among thousands of customers of American IT firm ConnectWise.At the center of the FBI’s alert is Artex, an open-source, AI-powered penetration testing platform originally designed to probe network defenses. By linking Artex to frontier large language models from companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as open-source and foreign AI models, threat actors have been able to automate the discovery and exploitation of basic security flaws. "Since at least August 2026, a variety of malicious cyber actors have used Artex to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries," said FBI in its report.While federal officials noted that Artex-driven intrusions are often "noisy"—generating high volumes of network traffic that can set off security alarms—the software operates at a pace that routinely outstrips human response times. In several observed cases, attackers progressed from initial targeting to full system compromise in under three hours.Once aimed at a target, the software rapidly scans networks for low-hanging vulnerabilities, such as weak configurations, missing multi-factor authentication, or exposed passwords. Upon securing a foothold, the tool autonomously navigates internal systems to harvest sensitive databases, mailboxes, and credentials.Since Artex debuted publicly in July, its capabilities have been tied to several high-profile breaches. In South Korea, attackers leveraged the platform against multiple financial institutions lacking basic protections like multi-factor authentication, resulting in the theft of personal records belonging to at least 68,000 individuals. "As of early November 2026, researchers identified over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX console instances, with total deployments likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks," says FBI.The FBI also corroborated earlier intelligence from Microsoft detailing how threat actors—believed by Microsoft to be operating out of China—used Artex to infiltrate IT management provider ConnectWise. Through that breach, the hackers accessed the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 ConnectWise customers to exfiltrate data.Although the creator of Artex has since transitioned the software to a closed-source model in an effort to curb abuse, the FBI cautioned that earlier open-source versions remain widely circulated and easily accessible online. Compounding the threat, careless operational security by the hackers themselves has left hundreds of active Artex instances exposed on the public internet without password protection. Just last week, cybersecurity researchers discovered numerous unprotected deployments online—including the exact system used to orchestrate the attacks against South Korea—potentially leaving powerful, turnkey hacking infrastructure open to anyone who stumbles across it.FBI recommends organizations take the steps below to improve their security posture:• Restrict cloud administration, network device management, application publishing interfaces (Kudu/SCM endpoints), hypervisors, backup platforms, and other sensitive services to trusted networks,private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths.• Disable basic publishing authentication where not required; restrict access to deployment and publishing credentials; restrict SCM access to approved management networks or deployment infrastructure.• Consider deployment models such as run-from-package that reduce direct modification of deployedapplication files.• Establish governance around public IP allocation; require architecture review before workloads or management interfaces are exposed directly to the internet.• Move enterprise applications behind Zero Trust access solutions to eliminate external exposure where feasible.* Put guardrails around high-impact business APIs: rate limits, recipient limits, transaction thresholds, abuse controls appropriate to function; alert when application operates materially outside normal volume.* On partner and employee portals, alert on sequential lookups and unusually high numbers of records accessed per session; apply rate limits to affected endpoints; enforce server-side authorization for access to customer records and limit responses to fields required for the operation.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: A man bought a £2,200 used Ford KA that developed repeated faults; another customer discovered her £1,850 Fiat was a write-off, UK dealer convicted after refusing refunds
articles.summary: A Westbury motor trader has been prosecuted after refusing refunds to two customers who bought faulty or misdescribed cars.
articles.body: A Westbury motor trader has been prosecuted after refusing refunds to two customers who bought faulty or misdescribed cars. Benjamin John Meacham, 35, pleaded guilty to three offences at Salisbury Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday 18 August. One customer paid £2,200 for a Ford KA that developed repeated faults and later became a non-runner. Another paid £1,850 for a Fiat 500L, later finding it had been classed as a Category S write-off. Its history had not been disclosed before the sale, officers found. Meacham was fined £1,400 and ordered to pay a further £2,600 after a Wiltshire Council Trading Standards investigation.Customer reports repeated faults with £2,200 Ford Ka after purchaseAccording to Trading Standards South West, the first case involved a Westbury resident who bought a Ford KA for £2,200 in March 2025 after seeing it advertised on social media. During a test drive, the vehicle displayed a flashing odometer, and Mr Meacham assured the customer that it would be repaired.The release states that further faults developed after the purchase. The vehicle was returned for repair, but the defects remained unresolved. When the customer sought to reject the vehicle and obtain a refund, repeated requests were refused, and the vehicle later became a non-runner.Buyer discovers £1,850 Fiat 500L was a Category S write-offA second investigation concerned the sale of a Fiat 500L to a Melksham resident in June 2025 for £1,850, the source reports. After the purchase, the customer discovered that the vehicle had previously been classified as a Category S insurance write-off, which the release explains means it had sustained structural damage.Trading Standards officers found that this information was available when the business acquired the vehicle but was not disclosed to the customer before the sale, according to the release. When the customer attempted to reject the vehicle because it had not been accurately described, she was told that Mr Meacham could not refund her and could not take the vehicle back. The source adds that a subsequent written request for a refund received no response.Cllr Paul Sample, Cabinet Member for Public Protection, said consumers have "clear rights" when buying a vehicle from a trader and should be able to make informed decisions based on accurate information. He said motor traders must ensure vehicles are accurately described and must respect consumers' statutory rights when faults arise. He added that the council is committed to protecting consumers and will continue to investigate and take action against traders who engage in unfair trading practices.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Inevitable he will die in jail': Imran Khan's sons accuse Pak of torturing ex-PM
articles.summary: The sons of imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan have accused authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental
articles.body: The sons of imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan have accused authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental torture in Adiala Jail, warning that he could die in custody without urgent medical intervention.In an interview with Sky News's Mark Austin, Sulaiman Isa Khan and Kasim Khan expressed concern over the deteriorating health of the 74-year-old Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder, alleging that he was being kept in solitary confinement for 22 to 23 hours a day, with little human contact and no access to independent medical care."We can see the path that this is taking. It's inevitable that eventually he will die in this cell. He will be killed in this cell if he remains there any longer without proper treatment," the brothers said.They also alleged that prison authorities had instructed guards not to speak to their father, adding that the isolation was being used to exert psychological pressure on him."I mean, we've been saying this for months. They're torturing him in the cell. It's physical and mental torture. It's at a point where they've instructed the guards not to even speak to him while he's in the cell just to, you know, maintain pressure and mental pressure on him," they added.The brothers said authorities had failed to implement an August 18 Supreme Court order directing that Khan be shifted to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for medical examination and treatment. The order had also called for increased family access, including regular telephone conversations with his sons."Nothing's changed at all, despite an order from the Supreme Court back in August for him to be taken and treated at a private hospital called Shifa International, and for increased family access to his family, calls with us, regular calls with us. But none of that has been implemented. And his health has just continued to deteriorate," they said."His blood pressure is now dangerously high, at about 193, I think. So he needs to be treated at a private hospital immediately," they added.The interview comes as Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges through an open letter, seeking urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi. He said his blood pressure had risen sharply and doctors had warned of the risk of a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest.In the letter, released by his party and lawyer Salman Safdar, Khan also alleged that authorities had failed to implement the earlier hospital transfer order. "I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he said.However, Pakistan's cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed Khan's claims, saying he had received regular medical attention and had been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations. The government has also rejected allegations of solitary confinement and denied that Khan was being denied access to his family.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A four-year-old British-born girl was brought to India by her father in 2025 and left with grandparents; after three UK court orders, an Indian judge ordered her return to her mother by November 18
articles.summary: An uncertain child inside a courtroom has become the defining image of an international custody battle involving two parents, two countries and competing
articles.body: An uncertain child inside a courtroom has become the defining image of an international custody battle involving two parents, two countries and competing claims over her future. The girl, born in Britain but taken to India by her father in 2025, is at the center of a legal battle that has now reached a critical stage. Three orders from British courts had failed to bring her back, but the protracted custody dispute moved a step closer to resolution with the Punjab and Haryana High Court ordering that she be handed over to her mother.High Court orders child given to motherAs per the report of The Tribune and Times of India Chandigarh city report, Justice Vikram Aggarwal directed the father to hand over the custody of the child to her mother on November 18 at 11 am.The mother, who now lives and works in the United Kingdom, had filed a habeas corpus petition in the High Court seeking the return of her daughter. The court also directed the Senior Superintendent of Police, Nawanshahr and the jurisdictional Station House Officer to ensure compliance in case the father failed to comply with the direction. The judge stressed the importance of a peaceful handover, with the police in charge of ensuring the child did not experience unnecessary stress or trauma.The custody dispute that crossed bordersAccording to The Tribune, the girl was born in the United Kingdom in April 2022 and moved to India with her father in June 2025. The mother said the trip was presented as a summer holiday, but the child was never brought back to Britain. The father, however, left the girl with her paternal grandparents in India and returned to the UK prompting the mother to seek judicial intervention.The case then went to the High Court of Justice, Family Division, England and Wales, The Times of India Chandigarh city report added. The British court provided three major directives., First, on March 25 it provisionally found that the child had been wrongfully removed from Britain and the mother’s parental responsibilities had been interfered with.It reiterated its call for the child’s return on April 15. Second, on May 5, it extended the child's status as a ward of the court and ordered her return by May 20, seeking the help of Indian authorities. And third, the child was in India however, despite these directions. The mother approached the Punjab and Haryana High Court.Child's welfare paramount to parental allegationsThe father objected to the mother’s petition stating that the child had traveled to India with her consent and was now settled with his paternal grandparents. He also claimed to be the primary caregiver when they were in the UK, dealing with her daily needs including food, baths and dressing. The Tribune reported that the child had also been enrolled in a school in India. His legal team said that a habeas corpus petition was not appropriate in a parental custody dispute and the mother should seek remedies under the relevant custody laws.However, the High Court rejected this objection and ruled that habeas corpus proceedings could be entertained even when a minor was in the custody of a biological parent. The Times of India Chandigarh city report said that the court relied on precedents set by the Supreme Court but added that the welfare of the child should be the overriding consideration.The judge also dismissed the father’s claims that the mother’s personal relationship was evidence that she was unfit to care for her daughter.Why the court favored the motherAt the heart of the ruling was the girl’s age and British nationality. The court cited Section 6 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, which states that custody of a child below five years would ordinarily be with the mother. The court also examined the mother's British employment and support network and the father's Indian location. The Court recognized the love and care paternal grandparents could provide, but held that the immediate welfare of the child was best served by living with her mother.The judge also considered the mother's and daughter's interaction in the courtroom to assess their comfort and emotional connection, The Tribune reported.Visitation with daughter remainsThe High Court clarified that its decision was an interim custody arrangement and did not permanently determine parental rights. Both parents are free to approach a competent court for a final custody decision, and it has to be considered independently. The father has also been allowed to keep contact with his daughter. He could return to the UK and see her for two hours every Sunday under the British court’s orders, or speak to her by video calls. If he stays in India, video calls of 15 to 30 minutes have been permitted.Images Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A UK homeowner was ordered to pay his neighbours £260,000 in damages and remove cameras overlooking their property; after repeatedly breaching court orders, he faced 448 days in prison
articles.summary: A long-running dispute between neighbours in East Sussex resulted in a homeowner being ordered to pay £260,000 in damages and remove cameras overlooking
articles.body: A long-running dispute between neighbours in East Sussex resulted in a homeowner being ordered to pay £260,000 in damages and remove cameras overlooking the neighbouring property. However, the conflict continued even after the court imposed restrictions on his behaviour. Mark Gary Coates repeatedly breached the orders and was charged with a second contempt of court and sentenced to 448 days in prison. In June 2025 the Court of Appeal dismissed his challenge to the sentence, ruling the punishment meted out by the lower court was justified.Why the UK homeowner was ordered to pay £260,000 The dispute was between Mark Gary Coates and his neighbours, Janice Elizabeth Turner and Brian David Abernethy Greenwood. The row concerned property boundaries and involved claims of harassment under the Protection from Harassment Act 1997.The neighbours took legal action against Coates and his wife [Court of Appeal judgment Turner and another v Coates (2025)]. Her Honour Judge Venn of the County Court at Hastings ruled in the claimants’ favour after a 5 day trial on 22 September 2022.Coates was ordered to pay £260,000 in damages, plus costs. It also imposed a number of restrictions on his conduct including removing items placed on a neighbouring track and refraining from threatening behaviour toward the claimants.One of the key requirements was the removal of cameras and video equipment that had a view of the neighbours' property. Coates was also prohibited from filming, photographing or making audio recordings of the neighbours or their visitors.How did the dispute lead to the first prison sentenceThe restrictions did not bring the dispute to an end. Coates breached several of the court's orders, prompting his neighbours to bring the first contempt of court proceedings against him.The case was heard on 26 October 2023, after an earlier hearing had been postponed to allow Coates to obtain legal aid and legal representation. However, his solicitors stopped representing him shortly before the hearing, leaving him to defend himself.Judge Venn found several allegations proven and sentenced him to 252 days in prison for contempt of court.Coates subsequently challenged the sentence at the Court of Appeal. In December 2023, the appeal judges upheld the findings of contempt, apart from one ground, but ruled that the prison term was too long. They said a sentence of approximately 3 months would have been appropriate and ordered his immediate release, taking into account the time he had already spent in custody.However, the court also made clear that any further breaches of the injunctions could result in a substantial prison sentence.What happened before the second contempt caseThe dispute continued into 2024 with the financial orders made against Coates remaining unsatisfied. On 14 March 2024 a charging order was placed on his and his wife’s home, with the order being for the property to be sold. If the outstanding financial obligations were not met, the sale was scheduled to take place in June.Turner and Greenwood filed a second contempt application on April 17, 2024, claiming that Coates had continued to breach the original injunctions. The allegations range from April 19, 2023 through June 10, 2024 and include harassment, intimidation and property damage.The Court of Appeal judgment recorded several serious incidents. These included throwing stones at Turner, injuring her hand, breaking a greenhouse window and damaging Greenwood's car window. Coates was also accused of making a throat-slitting gesture towards Turner, driving his van towards Greenwood in an attempt to run him over, filming Turner and threatening to kill the neighbours.The situation escalated on 10 June 2024, just three days before the deadline for the sale of his home. Coates began destroying parts of his own property, threw roof tiles at Turner from his roof and crossed onto the neighbours' roof, where he removed and damaged tiles.The court arrived at the 448-day prison sentenceThe second contempt hearing took place on 17 September 2024. Judge Venn considered 20 alleged breaches and found 19 of them proven, including all four of the particularly serious incidents highlighted in the appeal judgment.The judge calculated individual prison terms for the proven breaches, amounting to 546 days. She decided that the sentences should run consecutively because the incidents were separate acts rather than a single continuous event.After considering the overall punishment and applying the totality principle, she reduced the combined sentence to 448 days, equivalent to 64 weeks.Meanwhile, Coates was also facing criminal proceedings involving some of the same incidents. He had been charged with dangerous driving, harassment and criminal damage and was remanded in custody in July 2024.At his criminal trial on 29 November 2024, he was convicted of criminal damage to both his own home and the neighbours' property but acquitted of the harassment charges. In March 2025, he received a four-year and 16-week prison sentence for criminal damage, with another three-year sentence running concurrently.The Court of Appeal rejected his challengeCoates appealed the 448-day contempt sentence on two grounds. He argued that the civil proceedings should have been postponed until the criminal case was concluded because both involved overlapping allegations. He also argued that the prison terms for the separate breaches should have run concurrently rather than consecutively.However, in its judgment handed down on 25 June 2025, the Court of Appeal dismissed both arguments.Lord Justice Birss, sitting with Lord Justice Zacaroli, said civil contempt proceedings and criminal cases have different objectives. Civil contempt proceedings are intended to protect the dignity of the court and to compel compliance with its orders. This means they are not automatically required to wait for the conclusion of related criminal proceedings.The judges also noted that a person being acquitted in a criminal trial does not automatically make an earlier civil contempt finding unjust. The two proceedings can involve different evidence and legal considerations. The criminal sentencing judge had also taken the earlier contempt sentence into account when deciding the punishment for the criminal offences.On the question of consecutive sentences, the appeal court found that Judge Venn had been entitled to treat the breaches as separate incidents.You use AI every day. articles.title: Met Police missed opportunities stop predatory detective who ran rape unit, BBC finds
articles.summary: Warren Arter used his position - running a team investigating sexual assaults - to target women.
articles.body:
Warning: Contains details of violence, coercion and sexual abuse - and strong language

The Metropolitan Police repeatedly missed opportunities to stop a predatory detective inspector from sexually exploiting women whose cases he investigated, including one who married him and later died in unexplained circumstances, BBC Panorama can reveal.

Warren Arter used his position - running a unit investigating sexual assaults in south-east London - to target women it was his job to protect.

Two women, speaking out for the first time, have told Panorama how Arter groomed them. One says he raped her.

In the case of his wife, Rebekah, he filmed her being sexually abused and distributed the footage. She died in Barbados two years ago, while on holiday with him. On Sunday, the BBC revealed how he lied about what happened on the Caribbean island.

There were multiple investigations into Arter while he was employed by the Met. Now the former detective who led one of them has told the BBC that senior bosses tried to interfere with his inquiries, despite him having found potential victims.

While Arter was suspended as a result of that investigation, he remained on full pay for seven years - before being sacked in 2023 for drug offences.

The following year, the Met - having learned of his wife's death in Barbados - arrested him on his return to the UK for sexual offences alleged by another woman.

Arter took his own life days later in HMP Wandsworth. Despite the evidence against him, the Met has not reviewed all the cases he handled.

In response to our investigation, the Metropolitan Police has for the first time publicly apologised to the women he abused. It said it was now working to examine Arter's electronic devices to identify if there are further victims and that it encouraged other women to come forward.

Panorama has uncovered several opportunities to stop Arter that were missed by the Met:

In 2010, medical staff found Arter alone with a woman in the toilets of a sexual assault referral centre hours after she had reported being raped. Despite the Met being told, this did not lead to an investigation

The Met received six corroborated intelligence reports into sexual misconduct by Arter between 2014 and 2018

The force failed to arrest Arter in 2024 after being told he had sent an illegal upskirting image, and only did so after Rebekah's death three months later

This last missed opportunity came after the Casey Review's conclusion that the Met was "institutionally misogynistic", as well as the convictions of rapist and murderer Wayne Couzens, and rapist David Carrick - both Met officers - and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley's promise to "lift the stone" and "tackle everything underneath it".

Panorama can now reveal that 21 potential victims of Arter were identified in an investigation by the police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC). The Met has not contacted all the women whose cases he investigated during his 20 years as a serving officer.

The upskirting image that was sent in March 2024 to a woman we are calling Layla should have led to Arter's arrest.

Bail conditions or custody would have prevented him from taking his wife, Rebekah, to Barbados.

On 28 June, Arter rang Rebekah's relatives from the island to tell them she had died.

Rebekah had been escaping an abusive relationship in 2006 when the Met put then-Det Sgt Warren Arter in charge of investigating her former partner.

Arter pursued Rebekah, they began a relationship and he quickly moved in with her.

Her now-adult son, Elliot, says Arter initially made his mum feel "safer" but that his behaviour soon changed.

"He'd say to her: 'Get in the kitchen, make my dinner you slag. Make me a tea you [expletive] bitch,'" Elliot recalls.

Arter would openly watch pornography on his tablet while he was in the living room with her, Elliot says.

He also collected urine from Elliot, claiming he was testing it at the police lab to help the boy's promising football career - but Elliot now suspects it was an effort to hide Arter's drug use.

Watch Panorama: The Predator in the Police on BBC One at 21:00 on Tuesday 17 November (not in Wales or Northern Ireland) or on iPlayer

The inquest into Rebekah's death heard evidence that use of sedatives had become so routine in the home she shared with Arter, that a daily smart-speaker reminder announced "G o'clock" - a reference to the date-rape drug GHB.

In the years before she died, Arter had filmed and distributed videos of his wife being sexually abused. The BBC has seen some of them.

Many show her unconscious or otherwise incapacitated while Arter insults her.

"You should get raped," he says, in one video.

In another, Arter can be heard speaking to a man behind the camera, asking him to be quiet and saying "they go mad otherwise" - suggesting the video was being made for a wider audience.

His crimes were so brazen that he sent abuse videos of Rebekah unsolicited to at least four women he knew.

Two were women whose cases he had investigated - one of them was Layla.

She had met Arter in 2010 after she reported being raped. His exploitation of her continued for more than a decade, up until she reported the upskirting image - which she had deleted - to staff from the IOPC.

Both Layla, and her adult daughter who was with her when she spoke to the IOPC, say she identified the woman in the photo as Rebekah - whom she recognised from previous videos.

The IOPC says the staff member has no record or recollection of being told the identity of the woman in the photo - and it did not have the authority to investigate as Arter was no longer a police officer.

It did, however, tell the Metropolitan Police about the upskirting allegation.

Arter's abuse could have been stopped more than a decade earlier - soon after he had met Rebekah.

He claimed their relationship had begun after a chance meeting on a night out, an account she corroborated, when he was questioned by the IOPC during an investigation started in 2017.

However, Panorama has learned Rebekah was bombarded with more than nine hours of calls from Met phone numbers in the three months following the conclusion of her case in 2006. We also know that Arter searched her name on Met computer systems without any obvious justification.

Officers have faced misconduct proceedings, even prison, for relationships which began in similar circumstances, but at that time Arter was not disciplined.

It is not clear when his bosses found out about the relationship, but some of his colleagues appear to have known early on.

The BBC understands that four officers told the IOPC investigation they believed Arter had met Rebekah on a case. One said they knew Rebekah had been a victim of domestic abuse, but they refused to sign a statement.

The Met told Panorama that the IOPC's subsequent report had found that Arter's colleagues knew of his relationship with Rebekah, but did not know he had met her in the course of his duties, therefore he was not subject to any misconduct proceedings.

None of the various investigations into Arter led to criminal charges before he was arrested in 2024. On one occasion, he even received a payout after being arrested for harassment.

The IOPC has now told the BBC that of 21 possible Arter victims it had identified by 2020, it assessed he had inappropriate contact or relationships with eight of them, including Layla and Rebekah.

Panorama has, however, learned of at least one more alleged victim who says she was groomed and sexually exploited over 12 years.

Former Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Dame Vera Baird, is calling for an investigation by an outside force into all the cases Arter handled throughout his career.

"If a doctor had been found to abuse one person, they would look at all his list from start to finish.

"It's quite outrageous - there will be women living now with trauma imposed by him on them."

When Det Insp Jaysen Veeren tried to investigate Arter a decade ago, he says senior Met bosses tried to interfere with his work.

Veeren was a fast-rising officer in the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards (DPS) - which investigates police misconduct - and says he was warned he would be a "fool" to join the team because of its reputation within the force.

"The DPS is referred to as 'the rats' - you eat your own," he says.

But when, in 2016, he intercepted a Crimestoppers tip complaining about Arter's conduct with victims, he recalls telling his boss: "This is the case that I joined for."

Initially, his investigation was well resourced and he travelled to Australia to interview a woman who said Arter had sex with her after she reported being sexually assaulted as a tourist in London.

"We had one victim and, all of a sudden, you've got a second, third," he recalls. "It was quite obvious you're dealing with a predator."

Arter had been able to visit many of the women alone. One woman told Veeren: "He may as well have walked into my house with his [penis] out".

Veeren eventually arrested Arter and suspended him in December 2016 but Arter's phone had been wiped.

He then designed a plan to contact all the women whose cases Arter had investigated, but says he was prevented from doing so and his team encountered "interference" from senior officers outside of the DPS.

Emails seen by the BBC reveal his investigation was likened to a "witch hunt" by a detective chief inspector, who questioned its justification with the Met "haemorrhaging talent". A chief superintendent told Veeren's boss that staff felt the case was a "fishing expedition".

The two senior officers - who have since left the force - told the BBC this was not interference and said they were acting on concerns of colleagues about how the investigation was being carried out.

Veeren says he felt unable to widen his investigation and examine all of Arter's cases.

He referred his case into Arter to the IOPC in the expectation it would do so, and later reported his concerns to the watchdog as part of a wider whistleblowing complaint - alleging corruption within the DPS.

He resigned from the force in 2019 when he discovered none of his allegations would be upheld. The Met says his complaints to the IOPC had either been disproven or not corroborated.

Layla says Arter's abuse has "ruined her life" and she still struggles to leave the house.

Fourteen years before she told the IOPC about Arter's upskirting image, Layla reported being raped in a hotel room by a member of staff.

Arter was put in charge of her case, as the rape unit lead. He immediately began to target her.

Within hours of their first meeting, Arter asked Layla to put her head in his lap and then he stroked her hair, while a PC drove them to a sexual assault referral centre.

There, Arter was found by staff alone in the toilets with her.

A doctor was so alarmed by his behaviour that she reported concerns to the Met about his intimacy with Layla.

Layla has told us that Arter remained present while she had an internal medical examination.

The Met failed to investigate or monitor the detective's ongoing contact with Layla, who at the time was a vulnerable alcoholic.

Arter visited Layla dozens of times over the next few months, she tells us, sexually exploiting her during what he described as "therapy time".

Panorama has learned that Arter told colleagues that Layla was becoming too attached to him.

He was commended for victim care in her case - just as he had been in the domestic abuse case of his future wife, Rebekah.

Even after Arter informed Layla that the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) had declined to authorise charges in July 2010, he continued to contact her - helping her with a successful compensation claim under a government-funded scheme.

After Veeren referred his investigation to the IOPC, the watchdog described Layla as having been "groomed" by Arter.

Layla says Arter, who by this time had been suspended, was telling her what to tell investigators. She did not provide them with a statement.

Despite Layla's known vulnerability, and the evidence against Arter, it took three years for a file of evidence about his sexual misconduct to be sent to the CPS, which then declined to pursue criminal charges in 2020.

It was a further three years before Arter appeared at a misconduct hearing - and only then for drug offences.

He was finally dismissed from the Met in 2023 - have received at least £300,000 in pay while suspended. He kept his pension.

However, despite having left the force, a decision to review Arter's alleged sexual misconduct was then made.

In March 2024, IOPC staff visited Layla at home. She revealed Arter had sent her the upskirting image. By this point, she says she had begun to "wake up" to Arter's exploitation of her.

The watchdog told the Met about the illegal image - but the force failed to arrest him.

The Met told Panorama this was because of human error when using a new crime recording system.

On 28 June 2024, Rebekah died in a hotel room in Barbados while on holiday with Arter.

Disturbed by the lies Arter was telling them - his account of what had happened kept changing - her son Elliot and daughter-in-law Lacey went to the couple's house in south-east London.

They say they found a variety of drugs and hidden CCTV cameras that Arter had rigged up.

They also discovered photographs of Rebekah naked and bruised, involved in sexual acts, seemingly taken without her consent.

On 2 July, Elliot and Lacey drove to Bexleyheath Police Station - the same station where Arter had worked.

Staff were initially uninterested in Rebekah's death thousands of miles away, say the couple - and it was only when they mentioned Arter's name that officers became interested. "It was like chaos," Lacey says.

The family say they were told the Met was considering sending officers out to Barbados to help the investigation.

However, the BBC has been told that a senior Met boss from its Gold Command group was briefed that evening about the incident, in light of Arter's alleged offending, and a decision was taken not to send officers to the Caribbean island.

The Met told the BBC it took this decision because no allegation of criminality had been made.

Later that week, the Met visited Layla and interviewed her about Arter, where she disclosed he had raped her on one occasion and sexually assaulted her on another.

Arter flew back to London from Barbados on 9 July and was arrested at Heathrow Airport, accused of rape, voyeurism and coercive control. He took his own life in prison three days later.

Neither the Met nor the IOPC has ever released their investigation reports into Arter's sexual misconduct - despite Freedom of Information requests by the BBC.

Arter was seen as the star detective in a unit lauded for its results investigating rape and sexual assault.

But the Met has never investigated that unit's "sanction detection rates" - the proportion of reported crimes for which action was taken against suspects.

In 2009, Conservative politician James Cleverly, then a Member of the London Assembly, said the unit had achieved rates of 96%.

This is despite the figure being three times the London average and at a time when some officers were known to be systemically manipulating the recording of offences. The Met says it does not recognise the 96% figure.

If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence , information and support is available at BBC Action Line

Dame Vera says there seems to be many missed opportunities to stop Arter, spanning from 2006 to 2024: "There must have been other people who knew exactly what was going on."

Rebekah's family say the Met should investigate whether other men helped Arter abuse her.

When she died the Met seized electronic devices from the house she had shared with Arter. Elliot says some of those devices have not been analysed in two years.

His solicitor says a public inquiry is needed to reveal the full extent of Arter's offending.

"It's a disgrace for the Metropolitan Police, and it's also a dirty secret - one they want to keep hidden," says Sophie Naftalin.

The Met told Panorama that Arter could have been arrested sooner and it was "deeply sorry" for the harm caused to victims by his repeated exploitation of his position for sexual purposes.

It acknowledged progress with Arter's devices had been slow but said it was now being prioritised, and it encouraged anyone else who believes they were targeted to come forward.

It added that the recording of rape cases was examined nationally in 2014 - and there have been significant changes to the scrutiny of crime figures.

The IOPC says it regretted that its investigation took three years but it was a complex case involving delays out of its control. It added that the allegations were treated "extremely seriously" and resulted in referrals to the CPS.

The CPS says it thoroughly reviewed this evidence but concluded there was no realistic prospect of conviction at that time.

It says it did charge Arter with misconduct in public office before his death in 2024.

In September 2025, the UK coroner in Rebekah's case issued what is known as a prevention of future deaths report.

It said there was a risk that further deaths could occur unless action was taken.

In response, the Met said it had already taken action to improve vetting and to tackle police officers abusing their powers.

The IOPC said information had not been made available to it at the time of a specific risk to Rebekah, and that it had since strengthened its safeguarding procedures.

Elliot says he has spent the past two years trying to get answers.

"I don't think I've grieved yet", he says.

"I don't know what will happen when that day will come."

articles.title: 'Look who it isnae' - Still Game set to return as stage show
articles.summary: Still Game Live: Heaven Sent will run for 10 shows at the Ovo Hydro in Glasgow in 2028.
articles.body:
Seven years ago, Scotland's most beloved pensioners climbed to the top of Ben Lomond and reached the big Clansman in the sky.

But now, Jack Jarvis and Victor McDade have been resurrected as Still Game returns to the stage for a special run of shows.

The stage show, Still Game Live: Heaven Sent, will have a 10-date run at the Ovo Hydro in Glasgow from February 2028.

Creators Ford Kiernan and Greg Hemphill joked they had a "fear of moving on" after announcing the characters' return.

The ninth and final series of the BBC comedy aired in 2019.

However, the last appearance of the duo came in another stage show, Still Game: The Final Farewell, later the same year.

Still Game duo say no more Jack and Victor

Jack and Victor return as Still Game becomes a comic book

Kiernan and Hemphill previously said the final series and stage show would be the "final nail in the final coffin".

They did adapt the series for a comic book , which was released in 2024.

In a statement, they said: "We had FOMO (Fear of moving on).

"Haud oan! Whit's been happenin? It's been far too lang…Craiglang."

Still Game first arrived on TV screens in 2002, although the characters of Jack and Victor previously featured in sketch show Chewin' the Fat.

Alongside old pals Winston Ingram, played by Paul Riley, tight-fisted Tam Mullen, played by Mark Cox, nosy Isa Drennan, played by Jane McCarry and shop owner Navid Harrid, played by Sanjeev Kohli, the comedy follows the lives of Jack and Victor as they navigate the fictional Glasgow suburb of Craiglang.

The death of most of the characters was teased at the end of the ninth season and confirmed in The Final Farwell.

The stage show centred on Clansman barman Boaby, played by Gavin Mitchell, joining some of the characters in heaven.

It has not been confirmed who will return alongside Jack and Victor for the new show.

The cast previously set a string of box-office records with their hugely popular live shows in 2014, 2017 and 2019.

articles.title: Naked calendar raises thousands for blood cancer charity
articles.summary: The calendar from a Somerset theatre group has sold copies as far away as New Zealand.
articles.body:
A nude calendar put together by volunteers has raised thousands of pounds in aid of the charity Blood Cancer UK.

The calendar was created by the cast of Glastonbury & Street Musical Comedy Society's (GSMCS) production of the musical Calendar Girls.

It features well known faces from the Somerset town, who this week handed a cheque for £3,000 over to the charity after selling hundreds of copies and collecting donations at their shows in April.

"We had such great fun staging the show and stripping down for the naked calendar, and we're hugely grateful to those who donated," said Mary Parker, who also produced the musical.

Bird 'flockdown' impacting egg and turkey sales

Bus wedged in garden hedge after veering off road

Disabled man wins council tax High Court battle

Teachers, doctors, midwives and business owners all took part in the photoshoot, which was inspired by the original Women's Institute group who did the same thing in 1999 to raise money for their local hospital.

The original group became famous for using typical Women's Institute items, such as cakes and knitting, to preserve their modesty and ultimately raised £6m for Blood Cancer UK.

That story was later turned into the 2003 comedy Calendar Girls and later a musical by the same name, which has been a regular feature in theatres up and down the country.

The Somerset ladies have also achieved some international fame, with calendars being sold to customers as far away as the Netherlands, Australia and New Zealand.

Blood Cancer UK was chosen as it was the charity the original calendar girls raised money for after one of their husbands died from non-Hodgkin lymphoma aged 54.

"I know how much effort goes into raising money, and I'm grateful to everyone at Glastonbury and Street Musical Comedy Society who put on the show and everyone who came along and gave so generously," said Jim Ledbury, former treasurer of the Yeovil and District branch of Blood Cancer UK.

"I know my colleagues will be delighted to see what you've done to support blood cancer research, a cause we've spent many years fundraising for.

"Every pound helps, and we really do appreciate it."

articles.title: Experts say Tollesbury bone find likely belonged to woolly rhino
articles.summary: Nature lover Paul Rowe wants a museum to put his find on display for educational purposes.
articles.body:
Museum experts believe a bone found on a beach could belong to a woolly rhinoceros that lived during the Ice Age.

In May, Paul Rowe was helping out with a bird breeding survey along the Tollesbury sea wall, in Essex, when he picked up an "unusually heavy" curved bone from the edge of the River Blackwater.

The 63-year-old brought it along to a geology event earlier this month, where curators from the Natural History Museum in London shared their exciting theory.

Neil Adams, the museum's curator for mammal fossils, told him that the creature had most likely lived "between 30,000 to 60,000 years ago".

He reasoned that the bone was too small to come from a mammoth, but too large to be from a bison.

Dr Roula Pappa, senior curator of fossil mammals collections at the museum, agreed after initial examination.

The pair believed it to be part of the pelvis bone.

The Ice Age began more than two million years ago, bringing colder conditions to much of the world.

Mammals like the woolly mammoth evolved to adapt to the cold and the species thrived for hundreds of thousands of years.

The woolly rhinoceros appeared later during the Ice Age and became extinct when temperatures rose more than 10,000 years ago.

It could grow to about 3.5m (11.5ft) in length, 2m (6.5ft) in height and to 2,700kg (425st) in weight, roughly the same as a Range Rover.

Rowe spends much of his time photographing the natural beauty at the Blackwater Estuary and posting content to his social media page, Tollesbury Walks.

But even he was taken by his latest find.

He said: "I mean, these finds normally happen when there's a sort of archaeological dig or a geological survey of say, an old ancient riverbed in Essex. That's when these fossils tend to come about.

"But certainly the odds of simply walking along the shore and coming across part of a woolly rhinoceros from the Ice Age is pretty unique."

"I wouldn't hold on to it," he said, adding that he would happily see it verified and put on a display for educational purposes.

Dr Mark Curteis, former curator for Chelmsford Museum and chairman of the Colchester Archaeological Group, called it an "interesting and unusual" find, but not a first.

"Remains of Ice Age prehistoric mammals have been found in gravel quarries and on the coast in a number of places in Essex where they have been eroded out of the cliffs or deposited by long shore drift from further afield," he said.

Curteis explained that remains would have been buried in ancient river gravels and sediments, then exposed by erosion along the coast.

He added that fossil mammal remains are often found on beaches in Clacton, Holland-on-Sea, Walton-on-the-Naze and Mersea.

articles.body: Robin Li, chairman and chief executive of Chinese technology company Baidu, warned on Tuesday that fears of an artificial intelligence (AI) bubble could turn into reality if massive investments in the technology fail to deliver higher revenues and profits for businesses, according to news agency Reuters.Speaking at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO summit in Shenzhen, Li said that despite substantial spending on AI, most companies have yet to see significant improvements in their revenues or profitability."If we fail to address this, the concern that AI might be a bubble could well become a reality," Li said.Explaining the structure of the AI industry, Li identified four key layers: chips, cloud infrastructure, large language models and applications. He noted that competition is currently most intense at the foundational levels, but said the industry's long-term value would ultimately depend on the application layer.Li emphasised that companies must focus on turning technological advancements into commercially viable products and services to ensure sustainable growth in the AI sector.He also highlighted Baidu's launch of a platform called "Token Exchange", which directly connects AI token providers with enterprise and individual customers. articles.title: In 2024, off California, scientists detected 10 DDT+ compounds in deep-sea fish near Catalina, then analysed 215 fish and sediment to examine a possible link between seafloor pollution and marine contamination
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking study, scientists have detected 10 DDT-associated chemicals in deep-sea fish near Catalina Island, highlighting the long-term impacts of industrial waste on marine life and sediment pollution in Southern California.
articles.body: Industrial waste dumped into the ocean can remain in the marine environment long after disposal stops. This has been a concern in Southern California, where decades of industrial activity left behind chemical pollutants, including DDT. More than 50 years after offshore dumping ended, scientists are still investigating how these substances affect marine life. The presence of several DDT-associated chemicals was confirmed by researchers studying deep-sea fish and sediment of Catalina Island in 2024. According to the study in Environmental Science & Technology Letters, the research team collected 215 fish from the water column above the San Pedro Basin, around Dumpsite 2. According to their results, 10 DDT+ chemicals were detected in marine organisms, whereas 15 were detected in the nearby sediment. Researchers found an association between DDT chemicals in deep-sea sediment and their presence in marine organisms, but the study did not determine how the chemicals move from the sediment into the food web.Researchers detected 10 DDT+ compounds in deep-sea fishThe findings appeared in 2024 in Environmental Science & Technology Letters in a research paper examining DDT+ contamination in deep-ocean sediment and marine life in the Southern California Bight. Researchers used chemical analysis to examine sediments and marine organisms from the Southern California Bight, focusing on the San Pedro Basin near the historical offshore dumping area. The researchers conducted their analysis using 215 fish from three species, namely: Cyclothone acclinidens, Melanostigma pammelas and Leuroglossus stilbius. The 215 fish were pooled into four composite samples for chemical testing: 61 shallower and 146 deeper C. acclinidens, six M. pammelas and two L. stilbius. In this study, 10 DDT+ were found in the biota, while 15 were found in the sediments.DDT+ is the broader group. It covers the DDT-related compounds that are routinely tested for, plus TCPM and other lesser-known DDT-related chemicals. Of the DDT+ found in the biota, there were 8 DDT-related and 2 TCPM (tris(4-chlorophenyl) methane) related. All 10 DDT+ compounds found in the biota were also present in the sediment, which brings the total to 15. Of those 15, 13 (87%) had already been identified in Southern California’s birds and marine mammals.Chemical findings pointed to a possible connection between sediment and fishThe researchers analysed fish obtained at various depths in order to determine the pattern of contamination in the marine environment. C. acclinidens and M. pammelas were collected between 546 and 784 meters, while L. stilbius was collected between 546 meters and the surface. Within that range, the C. acclinidens composite from the shallower layer (546 to 657 meters) had less total DDT+ than the composite from the deeper layer (657 to 784 meters). But both the TCPM-associated compounds were not detected in the surface-dwelling L. stilbius sample. These data do not show any consistent correlation between depth and contamination for all three fishes.TCPMs were found in every biota sample except the single L. stilbius composite, which contained neither of the two TCPM-related compounds. As these compounds were also found in deep ocean sediments, it was concluded that the seafloor could be one of the sources of contaminants getting into the marine food web. However, the exact pathway by which the compounds were transferred from sediments to fish was not determined in this study.Earlier research connected fish contamination with polluted ocean sedimentsA separate 2024 study, “The persistent DDT footprint of ocean disposal, and ecological controls on bioaccumulation in fishes”, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in November 2024, examined existing sediment and fish contamination data collected across Southern California. It was established that the closer the fish were to the regions with high concentrations of DDT in sediment, the higher the level of accumulation of the compound in fish. As demonstrated in the above-mentioned study, the consequences of past activities are still present in the marine ecosystem in the region, more than 50 years after the last industrial discharge in 1971. From the results of these studies, it can be stated that the deep-sea sediments are still one of the components of pollution of the waters of Southern California. Even though the process of movement of DDT+ compounds up the food chain is not yet entirely clear, the presence of the compound in both the sediment and marine organisms proves that its effects are still present. The PNAS paper compiled a database of decades of sediment and fish measurements. It found that DDX levels in fish rose with sediment contamination, though not in a simple, uniform way. The authors say ecological factors such as species and habitat use mattered only in context and that combining ecotoxicology with ecology will be needed to predict risk in undersampled regions and species.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ukraine strikes Crimea Bridge for second consecutive day as Russia reports record drone attack
articles.summary: Ukraine struck the strategically important bridge connecting Russia with Crimea for the second consecutive day on Tuesday, according to the peninsula's
articles.body: Ukraine struck the strategically important bridge connecting Russia with Crimea for the second consecutive day on Tuesday, according to the peninsula's Russian-backed governor, as Moscow reported intercepting a record 1,441 Ukrainian drones across 22 regions.Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-appointed governor of Crimea, said two people were killed in the latest attack and traffic across the 19-km bridge had been suspended. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine on the reported strike.The extent of the damage to the bridge was not immediately clear. The Kremlin had said on Monday that the first attack on the structure this week caused only minor damage.The latest strike came amid what Russia described as the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the start of the full-scale war in 2022.Russia reports record Ukrainian drone attackRussia's Defence Ministry said its air defence systems had intercepted and destroyed 1,441 Ukrainian drones across 22 regions. The figure surpassed Monday's record of 1,336 drones, according to ministry data.Russian state news agencies reported that air defence forces had repelled the attacks, which targeted multiple locations across the country.The industrial areas of Ufa and Salavat in the Bashkortostan region also came under a large-scale drone attack, according to state media reports citing local officials. The region is home to several oil refineries.Why the Crimea Bridge is strategically importantThe 19-km (12-mile) Crimea Bridge, which carries both road and rail traffic, connects the Crimean Peninsula with southern Russia. It has served as a key supply route for Russian forces operating in Ukraine.The bridge is also regarded as one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's signature infrastructure projects.Russia seized and annexed Crimea from Ukraine in 2014. Since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, the bridge has remained strategically important for Moscow's military logistics and its connection to the peninsula.The latest reported attack marks the second consecutive day of strikes targeting the key crossing, raising fresh concerns over the security of one of Russia's most important links to Crimea.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'We don't have data based on religion': UP CEO on claim 'Hindu voters' were deleted in SIR
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh's Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa on Tuesday said that the Election Commission's database does not contain information
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh's Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa on Tuesday said that the Election Commission's database does not contain information regarding religion or caste.During a press conference, Rinwa said it was impossible for the poll panel to conduct any analysis based on religion and caste using the electoral rolls."If you look at our electoral rolls or our database, they contain the following details for each voter: their name, the type of relationship, the name of the relative, their age or date of birth, house number, and gender," the UP CEO said."Our database does not contain information regarding religion, caste, or any other such details; therefore, it is impossible for us to conduct any analysis based on these factors using our electoral rolls," he added."We do not possess any data based on religion. Approximately 2 crore 58 lakh citizens living in Uttar Pradesh are currently not included in the voter list," he further said.This clarification comes days after Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath claimed that 1.27 crore Hindu voters were missing from the state's electoral rolls after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).Adityanath said the Muslim voter population had increased by 1.65 per cent after the revision, while raising concerns over the deletion of Hindu voters' names."That is why we also submitted our memorandum to the Election Commission. We submitted it asking what reasons led to this," Adityanath said."There are 66 lakh such voters. 55 lakh voters are those Hindu voters who are direct beneficiaries of government welfare schemes, yet their names are missing from the voter list. There are around 4.5 lakh voters aged 18 and 19 whose names are completely missing from the voter list," UP CM said.Uttar Pradesh's draft electoral roll, published on Tuesday ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections, has 13.58 crore voters, including 6.20 crore women, Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa said.This marks an increase of over 18 lakh voters since the Special Summary Revision (SSR) following the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) published in April, he said.Rinwa said the draft electoral roll under the Special Summary Revision (SSR) 2027 contains 13,58,68,905 voters, comprising 7,38,58,510 men, 6,20,06,353 women and 4,042 third-gender voters."The claims and objections period will remain open from November 17 to December 16, during which eligible citizens can apply for inclusion, deletion or correction of entries in the electoral roll through Forms 6, 7 and 8, respectively," Rinwa said.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
