articles.title: Protests flare in Philippines over Trump's visit and planned AI hub
articles.summary: Protests against President Trump's visit to the Philippines have popped up around the country, as local residents criticize a Trump administration project to...
articles.body:
Manila, Philippines — Protests against President Trump's visit to the Philippines have popped up around the country, as local residents criticize a Trump administration project to build an artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub just north of the country's capital of Manila.

In the opening salvo for Pax Silica, a U.S. State Department-led international initiative to secure non-Chinese supply chains for high-tech manufacturing, a more than 4,000-acre manufacturing hub is planned to be built in the Philippines.

Protesters in Manila on Monday held signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or a devil, and signs calling on the public to reject the Pax Silica initiative.

Critics argue the proposed industrial hub will displace farming communities and the Indigenous Aeta tribe, harm the country's water supply and represent U.S. imperialism over the Philippines.

"They have been grabbing our lands. They have been grabbing our economy. … Pax Silica is just for the U.S. It's not for us," said Maninging Vilog, a teacher and advocate for Aeta communities.

"If you look at the farmers, what do they care about AI? The people selling water … selling cigarettes, the people who drive buses. What do they care about AI?" said Kaiser Cortina, a 20-year-old protester.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., also a subject of the protests this week, supports the hub. He said in October he is "terribly excited" about the project's economic benefits, framing it as a "grand opportunity" for the country to move up the "value chain" by shifting into advanced manufacturing and research, according to PhilStar Global .

Marcos' administration has claimed the project could create 100,000 to 130,000 jobs.

A proposed 4,000-acre artificial intelligence hub north of Manila is drawing opposition ahead of President Trump's visit to the Philippines.

The project is part of Pax Silica, a U.S.-led initiative aimed at reducing reliance on China for critical technology supply chains.… pic.twitter.com/9BQJFClqL8

Over 25 countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative since it was announced by the U.S. State Department in December 2025, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Japan and India. The Philippines joined the initiative in April , leading the U.S. and the Philippines to announce plans for a manufacturing hub.

A State Department spokesman said that the Philippines proposed the site of the hub, and that it is up to them to decide under its own laws and timetable, whether and how to proceed. They added that the U.S. remains committed to their set goal to create skilled manufacturing jobs in the Philippines and a more reliable supply chain for both countries.

The U.S. has raised concerns for years about supply chains for the hardware that powers AI, including worries that China could get access to advanced chips. The issue has drawn new attention in recent weeks, amid revelations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset whose company was under investigation for smuggling chips. (The company has denied chip smuggling.)

Pax Silica participants signed a declaration on Sunday that sets out a "common understanding of the sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure that underpin" artificial intelligence supply chains.

U.S. and Filipino officials have said there aren't expected to be any big announcements about Pax Silica this week during Mr. Trump's visit during the ASEAN summit in Manila . The U.S. president is expected to meet with Marcos on Wednesday before flying to China.

CBS News has reached out to the State Department for comment.

Antonio Tinio, a member of the Philippine House of Representatives, said there aren't any specific votes on Pax Silica planned in the country's legislature, and claimed "it's far from certain" that the Pax Silica hub will start construction and be successful.

And he added that the critiques of the Manila hub mirror the anti-AI data center sentiment in the U.S.

"The opposition to AI data centers is global. … That was one of the big issues in your election. It's a big issue. There's a lot of opposition throughout Southeast Asia, including Malaysia and Indonesia, and also in the Philippines," Tinio said.

articles.title: A Washington boy who was autistic, nonverbal and legally blind died at 15 after years of abuse in his adoptive home; six years later, his estate and brothers secured a $49.33 million settlement
articles.summary: Karreon Adams-Franks was 15 years old, autistic, nonverbal, and legally blind when he died in his Vancouver, Washington, home in 2020 after years of abuse
articles.body: Karreon Adams-Franks was 15 years old, autistic, nonverbal, and legally blind when he died in his Vancouver, Washington, home in 2020 after years of abuse and starvation. Six years later, his estate and his two surviving brothers have secured a $49.33 million settlement from the State of Washington and Evergreen Public Schools, according to reporting by Oregon Public Broadcasting, KPTV, and the Davis Law Group.The settlement resolves claims that state child welfare agencies and the school district failed to act on repeated warnings before Karreon’s death. His adoptive parents were convicted in 2023 of homicide by abuse and criminal mistreatment, but the civil case focused on whether the institutions responsible for protecting children also failed him.What happened to KarreonKarreon was adopted by his biological aunt, Felicia Adams, and her partner, Jesse Franks. He and his two younger brothers lived in their Vancouver home, where attorneys said the boys endured years of abuse, including beatings, choking, confinement, and food being withheld as punishment.Karreon was completely dependent on the adults around him for daily care. At the time of his death on November 27, 2020, he weighed 61 pounds.In 2023, Adams and Franks were convicted of homicide by abuse in Karreon’s death and criminal mistreatment of his brothers. Adams was sentenced to 35 years in prison, while Franks received 30 years. The Washington Court of Appeals upheld both convictions and sentences in March 2026.The warnings the state receivedThe lawsuit alleged that the Washington Department of Children, Youth and Families and the Department of Social and Health Services received reports about the family as early as 2017. Two referrals that year alleged that food was being withheld from the children as punishment.On November 20, 2020, a relative told the state that Karreon looked like a walking skeleton and was falling down because of malnourishment. A social worker visited the home the next day and described him as very skinny, but the lawsuit said the worker did not arrange medical care or remove the boys from the home.Karreon died six days later. The family’s attorneys argued that the state’s failure to investigate properly and act on the warnings contributed to the harm the boys suffered.What schools knewKarreon and his brothers attended Evergreen Public Schools, including Shahala Middle School and Mountain View High School. The lawsuit alleged that staff documented concerns about the boys for years but did not report suspected abuse to law enforcement or the state.In May 2018, one of the boys told a school bus driver that food had been withheld from him over an entire weekend. According to the lawsuit, the concern was relayed back to Felicia Adams, the person accused of abusing him, and the boy was beaten in retaliation.School records obtained by KPTV included an educator’s note saying that the parents withheld food as a form of discipline. Another note described Karreon eating breakfast and refusing to leave the table until he received more food.The settlement and who paysThe settlement was reached on October 8, 2026, days before a trial was scheduled to begin in Clark County Superior Court. It resolves claims brought by Karreon’s estate and his two surviving brothers.The State of Washington agreed to pay $25 million, while Evergreen Public Schools is paying $24.3 million. The school district’s payment represents the full amount of insurance coverage available to it, according to the Davis Law Group.Evergreen said the decision to settle was made by its insurers to avoid the risk of a jury verdict exceeding the district’s available coverage. The district said it maintained that none of its staff failed to make a mandatory report to the state or law enforcement.What the district saidIn a statement, Evergreen Public Schools said it recognises the profound loss of Karreon’s life and the lasting impact on his family. The district described the situation as tragic and said the perpetrators of the crimes are in prison.The district also said it hopes the settlement will allow Karreon’s brothers to continue healing without having to endure a trial. It said the staff who worked with the three boys were caring and dedicated educators who had the boys’ best interests at heart.The school district’s statement did not dispute the settlement itself, but it pushed back on the claim that staff failed to meet their reporting obligations. The distinction matters because the civil case was about institutional responsibility, not just the actions of the adoptive parents.Why the case mattersThe settlement highlights the role that schools and child welfare agencies can play in identifying abuse before it becomes fatal. Under Washington law, school employees who have reasonable cause to believe a child is being abused or neglected must report it to law enforcement or the state.Attorney Chris Davis said, as per the reports, that no amount of money can make up for what happened to Karreon and what his brothers endured. He said the people and agencies responsible for protecting them saw warning signs for years and did not act.For Karreon’s brothers, the settlement may provide financial stability and support for recovery. For the wider community, it serves as a reminder that every warning sign deserves serious attention, because a child’s life may depend on it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Neets review at a glance: Key proposals from Alan Milburn's report
articles.summary: A major review proposes widespread changes to help get young people into work across the UK.
articles.body:
A major review by former minister Alan Milburn has proposed widespread changes to help get young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) into work across the UK.

His report - which has now been published in full - says the UK should aim to reduce the rate of Neet young people from 13% to about 5% by 2036.

Its proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

Here is a summary of the key points from the review:

Major report proposes welfare changes, apprenticeships and tax cuts to help 440,000 young people into work

Young people should have a legal right to a route into education, training or work, and would be supported to do so under an "opportunity guarantee"

A new, locally-led Youth Opportunity Service in England would give young people one named advisor and a personalised participation plan - spelling out what action needs to be taken, by whom, and when

Tax, spending and other policy decisions should be put through a "youth opportunity test", to ensure they consider impact on younger generations

Prevention should start early, with primary and secondary schools required to identify and support pupils at risk of becoming Neet

Schools would also be required to offer work experience

A new performance measure would assess schools based on where their pupils end up

A new writing, numeracy and oracy check for pupils in Key Stage 3 (Years 7 to 9)

An extra 150,000 18- to 24-year-olds studying further education courses at colleges and other training providers each year

College funding to be based on how students perform and where they end up, rather than on how many students there are

A new digital open college, part-funded by employers and private investors, which would allow young people to study courses from colleges and universities

Aim to double the number of young people completing apprenticeships over the next decade - with more than a third of young people starting one every year

Where has the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds? Use our look-up to find out

The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis

An extra 170,000 job and apprenticeship opportunities to be created through employer incentives

Employers who take on any young person who has been Neet for six months should receive a £3,000 payment

Small businesses - with fewer than 50 employees - which do so should receive an extra £2,000

There would be an extra £2,000 payment if the young person has been in care or is disabled

Lower National Insurance costs for 21- to 24-year-olds, starting in retail and hospitality

Large employers should tell job applicants when they are unsuccessful

Young people who are already Neet should have guaranteed access to fast-track services like talking therapies and counselling within three months

These should be accessible without a diagnosis

A new digital-first mental health care service should be the "starting point for young people to access help"

The government should introduce national maximum waiting times for young people's mental health care from 2028

Fitness to work, or "fit notes", to be issued through the new Youth Opportunity Service, rather than GPs

An "entirely new benefits system" for under-25s

Young people to no longer get the health top-up of Universal Credit, which provides extra money for people whose health conditions limit their capacity to work

They would also no longer receive Personal Independence Payments (Pip), which help with the extra living costs of having a long-term health condition or disability

Instead, a new youth allowance would be set at the basic rate of Universal Credit for under-25s, with a higher rate for those living independently

A "local flexible health and disability fund" to be run by the local Youth Opportunity Service would pay for extra costs while a young person is receiving support

An additional cost allowance would replace Pip, providing "targeted financial support where disability-related extra costs are well established, significant and ongoing"

A new severe and complex needs insurance for those who will never be able to work

articles.title: Government must act now or lose Royal Mail, former minister Peter Kyle warns
articles.summary: The former business secretary says "undercutting" by rivals will make Royal Mail "unviable".
articles.body:
Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle has said the government must act urgently to "level the playing field" for Royal Mail or risk the business becoming unviable.

He said he was concerned that the firm was being "undercut" by rival parcel delivery firms who did not employ staff under the same conditions.

Royal Mail, which is owned by International Distribution Services, has struggled in recent years with increased competition, fewer letters being sent and fines from the regulator for missing delivery targets.

A government spokesperson said it would consider whether further reforms are required to the parcel market after the watchdog, Ofcom, publishes its annual monitoring report in December.

Kyle had started to prepare officials at the Department for Business and Trade (DBT) to look at the delivery market for parcels shortly before he was replaced in his job by Jonathan Reynolds as business secretary in July.

He said a "crunch point" had been reached where the government had to make a decision about whether it wants Royal Mail "to be a viable proposition in the future".

He said his review would have looked at where the costs in that market lay and where the profit was being made, to see successful companies upheld "the values of business in Britain today".

"If we leave it another few years then Royal Mail will just become unviable and it will just collapse under the weight of having full-time employees," he said.

According to Royal Mail, 98% of its 130,000 workers are permanent employees, with rights to benefits including pensions, sick pay and holiday pay.

Some other parcel delivery companies use self-employed delivery drivers, with some offering an opt-in service that gives couriers limited additional benefits.

Royal Mail is also legally obliged to offer customers a "one price goes anywhere" service across the UK and to deliver first class letters six days a week to every address.

Kyle's proposed review would not have considered further changes to Royal Mail's universal service obligations or to terms and conditions for its staff.

Royal Mail's performance has improved in recent months but it is still missing its targets for delivering first and second class post.

The firm was fined £21m in October 2025 for missing delivery targets in 2024/25.

Ofcom agreed last year to scrap second class deliveries on Saturdays and to reduce the target for delivering first class post within a day of collection to 90%.

A government spokesperson said the current business secretary had met Royal Mail and the Communication Workers Union, which represents postal workers, last week "to seek timely progress on improving their quality of service and to reiterate our commitment to the company's success."

DBT has also launched a consultation on tackling what it calls "bogus" self-employment, which it describes as "a practice whereby some businesses mislabel staff as self-employed to avoid statutory obligations".

Royal Mail has welcomed the consultation, and a spokesperson for the company claimed some parts of the delivery industry were "driving a race to the bottom" on employment standards and said it would "continue to push for a level playing field, with strong and enforceable standards across the industry."

Royal Mail misses delivery targets again but hails 'encouraging' signs

Hundreds of Royal Mail staff quitting each week under new efficiency plans

Many MPs across the UK have reported receiving high volumes of complaints from constituents about missed and delayed deliveries.

Shadow business minister Bradley Thomas said that Royal Mail's management needed to address the business's failings.

"Customers are being asked time and time again to pay increased prices, yet the service they're receiving is not improving," he said.

"Be in no doubt, this is not the fault of the hardworking postmen and women, it's the fault of Royal Mail's management.

"Nationalisation isn't the solution to this problem. Instead, we need ministers and Ofcom to bear down on Royal Mail's management to ensure they deliver on the improvements they've promised their customers."

The Communication Workers Union, which represents Royal Mail workers, is also putting pressure on ministers, with General Secretary Dave Ward calling for a "new model of ownership".

articles.title: Gunmen kill Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez
articles.summary: Rodríguez had denounced alleged links between criminal organisations and powerful figures in Costa Rica.
articles.body:
A Costa Rican journalist who denounced alleged links between politicians and drug traffickers in the Central American country has been shot dead.

Police said gunmen on a motorbike ambushed Camilo Rodríguez, 50, as he was travelling in his car north of the capital, San José, on Monday afternoon.

The independent reporter earlier said he had been receiving death threats from drug trafficking gangs.

Local media reported that it was the first murder of a journalist in more than two decades in Costa Rica. It comes at a time when transnational crime gangs are increasing their presence in the country, driving up its formerly low homicide rate.

The president of the Costa Rican Journalists' Association, Yanancy Noguera, said that "all evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice in Costa Rica - a person who published information about organised crime in the country".

Rodríguez had been working as a journalist for several decades, both in radio and in print.

Most recently, he had been uploading videos to social media in which he named public figures such as judges, business people and politicians, which he alleged were corrupt or had ties to known drug traffickers.

In one of his videos, he alleged that the home of Costa Rica's President, Laura Fernández, had been constructed by a company that he said had links to a criminal gang.

Fernández, who categorically denied any wrongdoing, took the journalist to court, accusing him of defamation.

Reacting to his murder in a video message, the president strongly condemned the attack, calling it "a stain on freedom of expression".

She added that she had instructed police to do their utmost to "punish Camilo's murderers".

Rodríguez had also tried to stand for political office, seeking to run as the presidential candidate for the Costa Rican Renovation Party in 2021.

However, his candidacy was rejected by the electoral authorities after the party failed to meet the necessary criteria required to file candidates.

Costa Rica's Attorney General, Carlo Díaz, said that "silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society".

articles.title: Hot weather delays Telford Town Park maintenance projects
articles.summary: Volunteers say the ground was so hard they could not dig during the summer months.
articles.body:
Park volunteers are still working on summer maintenance and improvement projects, after their efforts were put on hold because of the extreme heat.

In September, provisional data from the Met Office showed summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record - spring and summer saw persistent heat with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F).

Telford Town Park had to hold up projects including plans to revamp the sensory garden, and improvements around the Glade, the North Bank, Grange Pool and The Crannog.

"It's very frustrating, the ground being hard we couldn't do any digging," said Adrian Smith from the Friends of Telford Town Park.

"The sun has been quite a challenge for us, and we have lost a few plants throughout the gardens.

"This year has been a difficult year for us."

Some of the projects may not be completed until spring 2027.

"The one good thing about the summer was we had lots of tomatoes and cucumbers in the polytunnel," Smith said.

"We probably produced something in the region of 100kg of tomatoes, and I dread to think how many cucumbers."

The produce was donated to a nearby cafe, he added.

There are 25 volunteers in the group, who meet every Wednesday, and are now resuming summer jobs that were left unfinished - just as winter approaches.

"We're just starting to get back into it now, really, so the sensory garden is coming to a conclusion," he told the BBC.

"A lot of work has gone into ensuring there are sounds, smells and colours there, getting the stream flowing again and bringing some of the park's features back to life - we are now just working on the grass area."

Work has also resumed in the Grange Pool area.

"We've now produced the new dead hedge down there, we've widened the path… all the way around so it's now wheelchair accessible."

"We're working on replacing posts in the learning zone and will be pleased when we're finally able to host educational talks there, as well as able to ensure the Grange area is rewilded for insects and the north bank is suitable for lizards, with water flowing in the stream, there is a lot to look forward to."

However, Smith said the winter months were not without hurdles.

"The leaves are now falling quite dramatically, so a lot of our time now is spent cleaning up leaves and keeping the path clear so it's safe for the public to walk around," he said.

"There will be more challenges in the coming months for us."

Where else has been affected by hot weather?

Telford is not the only place where hot weather has affected how teams work on public spaces.

The authority said it had seen recent rapid grass growth due to an "unusually dry summer followed by warm, wet conditions".

During the prolonged dry spell in the summer, grass cutting was scaled back, while some work which usually takes place later in the year - like path tidying and hedge cutting - was brought forward.

The council added that it would look at how its planting schemes, grass management and wider maintenance programmes could be adapted to "remain resilient to increasingly variable weather conditions."

articles.title: After a fence dispute, an Ohio homeowner publicly criticised the city council president, who sued him for defamation; the appeals court reversed the lower court’s decision and sent the case back for reconsideration
articles.summary: A Hudson homeowner spent months criticising the city’s council president, Christopher Foster, at public meetings.
articles.body: A Hudson homeowner spent months criticising the city’s council president, Christopher Foster, at public meetings. The council president sued him for defamation. On Thursday, 12 November, the Ninth District Court of Appeals in Summit County overturned a lower court’s ruling on Ravida’s request to end the case early. The lower court had not explained its reasoning clearly enough for the appeals court to review. The case now goes back for a more detailed decision, and the question of whether Ravida’s words were defamatory remains unanswered.A fence dispute that started it allThe dispute began in 2023, when Anthony Ravida, a Hudson homeowner, asked the city for permission to build a fence. The fence he built did not meet the city’s codes, and he refused to fix it. A jury later convicted him of a zoning violation, and he appealed. While the appeal was pending, he began attending council meetings and using the public comment period to talk about his case. During meetings in early 2025, the homeowner stated that his conviction for violating the zoning code was based on a “false narrative” created by the city manager and council president. The homeowner also claimed that Foster was “basically above the law”, as the council president had the city repair his driveway without a permit. By May, he was calling for Foster to be suspended, investigated by the state attorney general and possibly removed from office. He also called him corrupt.The council president defended the city’s actions on the record. Foster stated that Ravida’s fence plainly violated zoning rules. He also responded to the homeowner’s allegations: “Yeah, simple issues, blown into conspiracy theories about taking bribes, getting kickbacks from people for putting sidewalks around the community really is pretty sad but I appreciate you coming out here and straightening that out.” The city manager said the driveway work was an emergency repair following a sinkhole in the public right of way. A construction company owner later told the council that a combination of personal circumstances and miscommunication had led to the permit being missed, and she denied any intentional wrongdoing.The defamation suitIn May 2025, the council president filed a civil complaint against the homeowner, alleging defamation and false light invasion of privacy. The homeowner asked a judge to dismiss the case under Ohio’s Uniform Public Expression Protection Act, a law that took effect on 9 April 2025. The law is intended to protect people from expensive lawsuits over their speech on public matters. The trial court said the law applied only to statements made after the Act came into effect. It dismissed claims based on name-calling, such as calling Foster a liar or a thief, ruling that these were opinions. It retained claims based on accusations of bribery and fraud, finding that factual disputes remained to be resolved. For statements made before 9 April, the court did not apply the new law at all.Appeals court calls for reconsiderationThe appeals court reversed the lower court’s ruling, finding that it had not properly applied Ohio’s Uniform Public Expression Protection Act (UPEPA). The trial court had applied the law only to statements the homeowner made after 9 April 2025, even though Foster had filed the lawsuit after that date. The appeals court also said the lower court had not properly explained its decision or addressed the arguments made by both sides. It sent the case back for “a sufficiently detailed judgment entry” that would allow meaningful review.The appeals court also said the trial court was wrong to exclude the earlier statements. The lawsuit was filed after 9 April, and the law states that it applies to civil actions filed on or after that date.The appeals court did not decide whether the homeowner’s statements were defamatory. That question still needs to be examined by the trial court. The appeals court’s ruling was supported by two judges, while the third agreed with the judgment but not the reasoning. The case now returns to the trial court.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Nvidia forms security committee amid 'spy' scandal  involving ex-CEO Jensen Huang
articles.summary: Nvidia has set up a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance, following reports about former CEO Jensen Huang's
articles.body: Nvidia has set up a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance, following reports about former CEO Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of links to the illegal diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to China.The company said on Tuesday that its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee would oversee its national security policies and compliance with export controls, as cited AP.The committee will be chaired by Nvidia director Suzanne Nora Johnson, with fellow board members Stephen Neal and John Dabiri as its other members. It will meet at least once every quarter and work with independent third-party experts to strengthen the company's existing national security and global trade compliance efforts.The committee will also work with independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts to oversee Nvidia's compliance programmes."We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation,” Chairman Harvey Jones said in a statement.US President Donald Trump welcomed the move, describing the committee as a positive step shortly after arriving in the Philippines on Tuesday evening.“Yes, that’s a good idea. It’s a great company,” Trump said during a photo opportunity in Manila with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan. “It’s a great idea.”The move comes amid scrutiny of Nvidia's chip exports to China and reports concerning Huang's relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who previously headed Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International. The company is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of US export controls.Nvidia's advanced chips are in high demand because they power cloud computing and data centres that support the artificial intelligence industry. However, their sale to China is subject to US export restrictions.Reports about Huang's alleged relationship with the businesswoman, including claims that she was a suspected Chinese spy, have also raised questions about potential national security risks and oversight of the company's chip exports.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: ​In 2016, Gina Rinehart's group acquired a controlling stake in the Kidman cattle empire; a decade later, it is selling the 623,000-hectare Queensland station, which has 15,000 cattle and is valued at more than A$55 million
articles.summary: Billionaire Gina Rinehart is selling Morney Plains Station, her 623,000-hectare cattle property in southwest Queensland.
articles.body: Billionaire Gina Rinehart is selling Morney Plains Station, her 623,000-hectare cattle property in southwest Queensland. The off-market sale could fetch more than A$55 million, according to a report by the Australian Financial Review. The sale is being handled by Elders Real Estate agent Tom Russo.Morney Plains Station sits in the Channel Country near the South Australian border, about 230 kilometres east of Birdsville, and spans three titles. A herd of around 15,000 cattle runs on the property, and Wagyu bulls were recently introduced. The property is more than twice the size of the Australian Capital Territory.The sale is part of a broader shift at S. Kidman & Co, in which Rinehart's group holds a majority stake. Adam Giles, the former Northern Territory chief minister who runs Hancock Agriculture and S. Kidman & Co, told the newspaper that the group is seeking to repurpose some of its capital. “An opportunity has come up, and we’re seeking to repurpose some of our capital with different investments within agriculture to better diversify our approach.”The sale comes as the billionaire shifts her investments towards more premium, higher-priced beef production.How it startedThe deal that started it all was struck in 2016. Hancock Prospecting and Chinese company Shanghai CRED bought S. Kidman & Co in 2016 for A$386.5 million. Hancock took a 67 per cent stake, while CRED owned the remaining 33 per cent. The Australian government approved the deal in December that year. The company has since sold several cattle stations. Kidman was once the country's largest private landholder. By April 2023, it had sold four stations and was left with four properties covering around two million hectares: Helen Springs in the Northern Territory, and Morney Plains, Rockybank and Durham Downs in Queensland.Morney Plains is the second Queensland station the company has put on the market this year. Kidman also sold the Rockybank aggregation to local farmers in June for more than A$60 million, the outlet reported. The upcoming sale is off-market, which means there is no public listing or advertised price. It is important to note that the A$55 million figure is an estimate, not a confirmed valuation. The buyer will acquire a cattle station with limited carrying capacity in a region where rainfall is often unpredictable. However, a Wagyu breeding programme is already underway.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2021, singer Charlotte Church bought the former Welsh home of fashion designer Laura Ashley and turned it into a wellness retreat; five years later, the project that hosted more than 3,000 guests is closing for good
articles.summary: Discover the closure of Charlotte Church's wellness retreat, The Dreaming, which offered holistic experiences and welcomed over 3,000 guests before ending its journey.
articles.body: A historic Welsh property that became a destination for relaxation, nature and spiritual healing is preparing to close its doors permanently. Singer Charlotte Church's wellness venture, The Dreaming, welcomed thousands of guests over five years, offering an alternative retreat experience built around nature, community and personal wellbeing. However, what was initially announced as a temporary break from operations has now become a permanent goodbye.According to an announcement published on The Dreaming's official website, the retreat is ending its journey after five years, with more than 3,000 people having visited the property during that period. Church bought Rhydoldog House, the former home of fashion designer Laura Ashley, in 2021 and transformed it into a wellness destination. The closure announcement follows an earlier decision to pause operations and reconsider the project's future.How Charlotte Church transformed Laura Ashley's former homeChurch purchased Rhydoldog House near Rhayader in Powys, Wales, in 2021, reportedly for around £1.5 million. The property had previously belonged to fashion designer Laura Ashley and her husband, Bernard Ashley. The singer was drawn to the surrounding landscape, which included woodland, gardens, streams and natural spaces. She envisioned creating a place where visitors could disconnect from everyday pressures and reconnect with themselves and the environment.The transformation of the historic property involved extensive renovation work, which was also documented in a Discovery Channel television series. Church eventually established The Dreaming, which opened as a wellness retreat in 2023. The property offered accommodation and experiences designed around holistic wellbeing. Its facilities included gardens, communal spaces, a healing room, a Japanese tea house and outdoor areas where visitors could spend time in nature.Retreat offered nature-based experiences and affordable staysThe Dreaming was designed to offer more than a conventional hotel or spa experience. Its programmes included sound healing, yoga, forest bathing, meditation, creative activities and Druid ceremonies. Guests were also encouraged to participate in communal meals, spend time outdoors, explore the surrounding woodland and take part in activities that promoted relaxation and connection.According to the Shropshire Star's October 2026 report, the retreat had introduced a pay-what-you-can arrangement, allowing visitors to book certain spaces for as little as £1 per night. NHS workers were also offered free stays. The initiative was intended to make wellness experiences accessible to people with different financial circumstances rather than limiting them to visitors who could afford expensive retreats. Over five years, more than 3,000 guests visited the property, according to the organisation's final announcement.Why Charlotte Church decided to close The DreamingThe closure followed an announcement in October 2026 that The Dreaming would pause its operations from December to reconsider its future. At the time, the retreat described the decision as a period of hibernation, saying it needed time to reflect on what it should offer and how it could continue serving people amid changing circumstances. However, its latest statement confirmed that the pause would not lead to a reopening. In its announcement, the team said it had initially hoped the break would create space for new possibilities but had eventually realised that it marked the end of the project.The statement also reflected on the experiences shared by guests, including gatherings around fires, cold-water swimming, woodland walks, communal meals, music and storytelling. It thanked the volunteers, artists, gardeners, chefs, housekeepers and other team members who helped establish the retreat.Church had previously described the project as a response to the pressures of modern life. Speaking to the Press Association, she said people increasingly needed care, community, nature and a sense of belonging.Although The Dreaming is closing, its official announcement expressed hope that visitors would carry the experiences and connections they developed there into their everyday lives. The organisation described the five years as a special chapter and thanked everyone who had supported its journey.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Speed camera fault may have allowed drivers to escape fines
articles.summary: The Home Office has revoked approval that allowed footage from speed cameras to be used in evidence.
articles.body:
Further problems with the accuracy of speed cameras on English roads have been uncovered which may have allowed drivers to slip through the cracks and escape fines.

National Highways discovered issues with speed cameras last year , affecting 154 out of 400 cameras but, following an investigation, said it had found another fault on units monitoring roads including those running between Huntingdon and Cambridge.

The Home Office revoked approval that allows footage from the cameras to be used as evidence in legal proceedings. US firm Verra Mobility operates the cameras but National Highways said it would now end its contract.

Roads minister Justin Madders said: "We can't take chances with this.

"If we're going to prosecute people, we need to be confident the system is working as it should. That's why we've taken the action we have."

The fault affected all of the variable speed cameras on smart motorways, and a section of the A14 between Huntingdon and Cambridge as well as the A1 approach junction to the A14.

A spokesperson for National Highways said that Verra's camera system had been selected on the basis that it maintained Home Office approval.

The agency said that since that was no longer the case "we are ending our contractual relationship to use the cameras for enforcement".

It added: "We are considering all further commercial and legal options that may be appropriate."

The BBC has contacted Verra Mobility for comment.

Madders said that the enforcement of speed limits continues to be conducted through a range of different tactics, including mobile cameras as well as marked and unmarked police patrols.

But he admitted that the camera system will not be fully fixed until sometime next year.

There are 4,000 cameras across the entire road network.

In December 2025, National Highways, which runs England's motorways, blamed an "anomaly" in how variable speed cameras were interacting with speed limit signs on some A roads and motorways.

For example, on a road where the speed limit increases, a driver may see a sign showing 60mph but the camera recording it may still be working on the basis of a previous 40mph speed limit.

The fault led to 2,650 wrongful speed camera activations between 2021 and the end of last year.

Those who had been wrongfully fined have been reimbursed.

As National Highways continued to test the system, it discovered a further problem "relating to how some of these cameras may activate in specific and rare circumstances".

It said that according to its calculations, "the circumstances in which the latest issue could occur are extremely rare, and there is no evidence to suggest it has impacted enforcement".

Nevertheless, it said it was "taking immediate steps to ensure compliance is maintained at relevant locations".

It said it would out further traffic officer patrols in place to monitor the sites.

articles.title: Five-year-old killed, brother injured in wedding firing
articles.summary: Five-year-old killed and three-year-old critically injured after alleged firing at Madhepura wedding venue post-vidai; police recover cartridges, hunt accused.
articles.body: Patna: A five-year-old boy was killed and his three-year-old brother critically injured after a man allegedly opened fire at a wedding venue in Madhepura on Monday night, shortly after the bride’s “vidai” ceremony.The deceased was identified as Mohammad Sarfaraz, son of Mohammad Sonajir, a resident of Roshanganj under Bhawanipur police station in Purnia district. His younger brother, Mohammad Ali Hussain, was shot in the abdomen. The children had accompanied their family to their maternal grandparents’ house for their aunt’s wedding.The accused, Mohammad Aurangzeb Alam, a resident of Gulab Tola, allegedly fired two rounds from a country-made pistol during the wedding procession. Family members and guests persuaded him to stop. However, after the procession left, he allegedly returned in an intoxicated state and opened fire, hitting the two children.They were taken to Jan Nayak Karpuri Thakur Medical College and Hospital in Madhepura, where Sarfaraz succumbed to his injuries. Ali Hussain was referred to a higher medical centre and remained critical.Police teams from Bihariganj and Manjoura reached the spot and launched an investigation. articles.title: Trump arrives in Manila ahead of talks with Putin and Xi in China
articles.summary: The US president said he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Russia's Vladimir Putin "if it's available".
articles.body:
President Trump has arrived in the Philippines' capital on the first leg of a trip to Asia, which will end in a meeting in China with its President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin.

A red carpet was rolled out for Trump as he walked off Air Force One in Manila. A band played one of his favourite songs, Y.M.C.A., before he was whisked away by helicopter to a hotel.

Trump's first meeting at the Asean Summit was with America's partners in the Quad - India's Narendra Modi, whom he described as a "very tough man", Japan's Sanae Takaichi, who "may be even tougher", and Australia's Anthony Albanese.

"Our countries are the four corners of the free, open, stable, prosperous Indo-Pacific," the US president said.

"We have outstanding relationships and co-ordinate closely... my phone is always open," Trump added.

Many countries in South East Asia have been hit hard by Donald Trump's tariffs and his war on Iran - but their exports to the US rose 30% last year thanks to the AI boom for which the region manufactures many of the components.

The US is hoping to draw more countries here into its "Pax Silica" tech and AI ecosystem, and away from China.

But China's huge influence in this region cannot easily be challenged, and certainly not in the few hours Trump is in the Philippines.

After an overnight stay in Manila, the US president will fly to Shenzhen in China to attend a summit of Asia Pacific leaders and have nuclear talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Asked if he would also be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, Trump said: "If it's available, I would".
